svg.title: Orion across the electromagnetic spectrum
svg.desc: Animated comparison of one patch of sky, the constellation Orion, in six bands of the electromagnetic spectrum, with a marker moving along a logarithmic wavelength bar (10 m to 1 femtometre). Star positions are real (J2000); the emission in each band is stylised in false colour from the classic surveys. Radio (λ ≈ 1 cm – 3 mm): Hot ionised gas in the Orion Nebula and cold molecular clouds (carbon monoxide at 2.6 mm). Stars are almost invisible. Seen by radio dishes and millimetre-wave telescopes. Infrared (λ ≈ 100 µm): Warm dust: the Orion A and B clouds and the ring around Meissa (λ Orionis). Cool Betelgeuse is the brightest star. Seen by the Infrared Astronomical Satellite (IRAS) and Planck. Visible light (λ ≈ 400 – 700 nm): Stars in their true colours: red Betelgeuse, blue-white Rigel, the belt, and the pink glow of the Orion Nebula. Seen by your eyes and every camera. Ultraviolet (λ ≈ 150 nm): Only hot O and B stars shine: Rigel, the belt, Bellatrix. Betelgeuse, at about 3,600 K, almost vanishes. Seen from space by the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX). X-ray (λ ≈ 1 nm): Million-degree gas: flaring young stars in the Orion Nebula Cluster and the hot Orion–Eridanus superbubble. Seen by Chandra and the Röntgensatellit (ROSAT). Gamma rays (λ ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m (GeV photons)): Cosmic rays smashing into the gas of the Orion A and B molecular clouds make a faint gamma-ray glow. Seen by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. References: Getman et al. 2005 (Chandra Orion Ultradeep Project); Burrows et al. 1993 (ROSAT, Orion–Eridanus bubble); Ackermann et al. 2012 (Fermi-LAT, Orion molecular clouds).
svg.text: ONE PATCH OF SKY · SIX WAYS TO SEE IT
